aspects.says: A Date holds only milliseconds since the epoch; toString(), the field getters and a SimpleDateFormat without a zone use the JVM's default zone, so the day of a Date depends on the zone you name.
basis: section:A Date Has No Zone; toString() Uses the JVM's Default

aspects.says: A java.util.Date can be changed with setTime by anyone holding it, so a class that keeps one copies it on the way in and on the way out.
basis: section:A Date Is a Mutable Moment, So Anyone Holding It Can Move It

aspects.says: A final Date field fixes which object the field refers to, not the moment inside it, and a getter that returns the field hands out that object.
basis: section:A Date Is a Mutable Moment, So Anyone Holding It Can Move It

aspects.says: SimpleDateFormat parses leniently by default, turning an impossible date into a real one.
basis: section:Parsing Is Lenient by Default, and Strict Mode Still Ignores What Follows the Date

aspects.says: A lenient Calendar, the default, carries out-of-range fields into the next field, so 30 February becomes 2 March instead of an error.
basis: section:Months Count From 0, Years From 1900, and Out-of-Range Values Roll Over

aspects.says: Calendar and the deprecated Date constructors and getters count months from 0, and Date counts years from 1900.
basis: section:Months Count From 0, Years From 1900, and Out-of-Range Values Roll Over

aspects.says: A SimpleDateFormat shared by threads returns wrong dates, most of them without any exception, because it parses into a Calendar of its own; DateTimeFormatter is safe to share.
basis: section:One SimpleDateFormat Shared by Threads Returns Wrong Dates

aspects.says: java.sql.Date extends java.util.Date but throws from toInstant() and the time getters, so code written for java.util.Date fails on values from ResultSet.getDate; a java.sql.Date names a day, read with toLocalDate(), not by shifting its milliseconds into another zone.
basis: section:java.sql.Date Is a java.util.Date That Breaks Its Parent's Contract

aspects.says: The java.sql.Date(long) constructor keeps the time of day, so two values that print the same day are not equal.
basis: section:java.sql.Date Is a java.util.Date That Breaks Its Parent's Contract

aspects.says: Even with setLenient(false), SimpleDateFormat.parse(String) ignores text after the date and does not enforce the pattern's widths; LocalDate.parse reads and validates the whole text.
basis: section:Parsing Is Lenient by Default, and Strict Mode Still Ignores What Follows the Date

aspects.says: TimeZone.getTimeZone returns GMT for an ID it does not know and still accepts ambiguous three-letter IDs.
aspects.reason: a lookup fact in the reference table with no section of its own; zone IDs are practised in unit 7.3.2.5
